blocks.text: Aristotle, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ἀπαίρουσι δὲ, etc. καὶ οὐ χειμάζουσι, καὶ αἱ χελιδόνες, καὶ αἱ τρυγόνες [Apairousi de, etc. kai ou cheimazousi, kai hai chelidones, kai hai trygones]; Both swallows and turtledoves depart, and do not winter among us. The author To Herennius: Swallows are at hand in summertime; driven off by winter, they withdraw. Pliny, book 10, chapter 24: Swallows too depart in the winter months. Damir: وهو من الطيور القواطع [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ] It is one of the migratory birds. Columella, in his prose On the Cultivation of Gardens, book 12, chapter 3: Soon, when the winter solstice is over, after an interval of forty days, around the arrival of the swallow, when Favonius is already rising. And book 10, chapter 14: While the rising of Arcturus and the arrival of the swallow promise more favourable weather. In Pliny, book 2, chapter 47: Some call Favonius, on the 7th day before the Calends of March, Chelidonias, from the sighting of the swallow. Favonius, that is, Zephyr. Hence Horace, book 1, Epistle 7, to Maecenas:
If you will allow me, with the Zephyrs and the first swallow.
And Oppian on the swallow, book 3 of the Halieutica, line 244:
— — εἰαρινὴ Ζεφύρου πρωτάγγελος ὄρνις, [eiarinē Zephyrou prōtangelos ornis,]
The spring bird, first messenger of Zephyr. And Nonnus, book 2 of the Dionysiaca:
— — εἰαρινοῖο φίλη Ζεφύροιο χελιδὼν, [eiarinoio philē Zephyroio chelidōn,]
The swallow, friend of the spring Zephyr. And in book 47:
Καὶ Ζεφύρου καλὸς ὄρνις ὑπωροφίην χέε μολπὴν, [Kai Zephyrou kalos ornis hypōrophiēn chee molpēn,]

And the beautiful bird of Zephyr poured out its song beneath the roof. As if alluding to the Greek proverb Νέα χελιδὼν [Nea chelidōn], A new swallow, which Suidas, by a lapse of memory, cites from the Birds of Aristophanes, although it is read nowhere but in the Knights, Act 1, in these words: [II, 611] Σκέψασθε παῖδες, οὐχ' ὁρᾶθ'; ὥρα, νέα χελιδὼν, [Skepsasthe paides, ouch' horath'; hōra, nea chelidōn,] [col. 66]

Look, boys, don't you see? It is spring, a new swallow. On which the Scholiast: Ἔστιν ἔαρος ἀρχή· δοκεῖ γάρ πως ἅμα τῷ ἔαρι φαίνεσθαι χελιδών. [Estin earos archē; dokei gar pōs hama tō eari phainesthai chelidōn.] It is the beginning of spring, for the swallow seems to appear together with the spring. So in the Birds (which may have misled Suidas) the appearing swallow teaches
Ὅτε χρὴ χλαῖναν πωλεῖν ἤδη, καὶ ληϊδάριόν τι πρίασθαι, [Hote chrē chlainan pōlein ēdē, kai lēidarion ti priasthai,]
When the cloak is to be sold, so that a summer garment may be bought. And in the Peace the Chorus sings:
— — ὅταν ἠρινᾷ μὲν [hotan ērina men] — — when indeed with spring Φωνῇ χελιδὼν [Phōnē chelidōn] voice the swallow Ἑζομένη κελαδῇ. [Hezomenē keladē.] sitting resounds.

Similar to which are these words of Stesichorus, as the Scholiast notes: Ὅταν ἦρος ὥρᾳ κελαδῇ χελιδών· [Hotan ēros hōra keladē chelidōn;] When the swallow shall resound in springtime. Nor are these words of Simonides in Athenaeus far off: Ἄγγελε κλυτὰ ἔαρος ἁδυόδμου κυανέα χελιδὼν [Angele klyta earos hadyodmou kyanea chelidōn], O famed messenger of sweet-scented spring, dark-blue swallow^{*)}. And in Theognis, book 3, on the sacrifices of the Rhodians, the song which οἱ χελιδονίζοντες [hoi chelidonizontes] sang from door to door, that is, the beggar-minstrels who announced that the swallow had come (in Hesychius χελιδονισταὶ [chelidonistai]), begins thus: Ἦλθ', ἦλθε χελιδὼν καλὰς ὥρας ἄγουσα, καὶ καλοὺς ἐνιαυτοὺς, ἐπὶ γαστέρα λευκὰ κἀπὶ νῶτα μέλαινα· [Ēlth', ēlthe chelidōn kalas hōras agousa, kai kalous eniautous, epi gastera leuka kapi nōta melaina;] The swallow has come, has come, with white belly and black back, bringing fair seasons and fair years. See the rest there. Accordingly, as Theon writes on Aratus, the ancients painted the northern Fish with a swallow's head and called it ἰχθὺν χελιδόνιαν [ichthyn chelidonian], because by its rising it signified the prelude of spring. To the same point belong these words of Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 52: Χελιδὼν δ' ἄρα τῆς ὥρας τῆς ἀρίστης ὑποσημαίνει τὴν ἐπιδημίαν· [Chelidōn d' ara tēs hōras tēs aristēs hyposēmainei tēn epidēmian;] The swallow signals the arrival of the most beautiful season of the year. And Ovid, almost at the end of book 2 of the Fasti:
Am I deceived, or has the swallow, harbinger of spring, come?
And Columella in the Garden:
And the swallow will have sung of spring's arrival from her nest.
And Calpurnius, Eclogue 5:
— — in early spring, when the birds are already beginning to twitter, and the returning swallow plasters her nests with mud.
And an unknown poet among the Epigrams of the ancients, book 4:
The frisky kid and the chattering swallow announce springtime, and the bowl of milk, and the green grass. [II, 612] And in book 5, Avienus:
For when in early spring the hard earth loosens itself, and the swallow, winged one, chirps sweetly in the hollow rooftops.
